review_evidence: Focused schema, runtime hash, pedagogy, freshness, coverage, and key self-review for eng_c4_ch06 on 2026-07-12
title: Braille
source_note: NCERT structural alignment only. Zidd uses original teaching passages, checks, and feedback instead of copying the textbook body.

levels.title: Understand how dot patterns carry meaning
levels.focus: identify the main idea and key details in an informational paragraph
levels.teaching_goal: Explain how organised raised-dot cells let a reader recognise letters, words, and signs by touch.

guided_check.teaching_block: The main idea joins the important details. Worked example: raised dots are arranged in small cells; each arrangement stands for something; fingertips detect the arrangements. Together, these details explain how Braille carries written meaning through touch.
guided_check.passage: Meera moves her fingertip across a row of firm dots. Each small group has a different arrangement. She recognises the groups as letters and reads the label without seeing it.
guided_check.prompt: Which statement gives the paragraph's main idea?
options: different raised-dot patterns can be read by touch
all labels must be made of paper
every dot group means the same letter
accepted_answers: different raised-dot patterns can be read by touch
raised dot patterns can be read by touch

bridge.teaching_block: Break the process into three parts: what is felt, how it is organised, and what it means. Raised dots + distinct pattern + letter meaning explains the system.
bridge.passage: One cell has two raised dots. The next has four in a different pattern. Arun feels the difference and identifies two letters.
bridge.prompt: What lets Arun tell the letters apart?

masterclass.teaching_block: Misconception check: Braille is not a row of random bumps and it is not a separate spoken language. The planned position of each raised dot represents written symbols.
masterclass.passage: A card contains several six-position cells. Some positions are raised and others are flat. Tara reads the cells as a room number.
masterclass.prompt: Why must the dot positions be arranged carefully?
options: each pattern represents a particular symbol
the positions make the card louder
accepted_answers: each pattern represents a particular symbol

independent_check.teaching_block: Read the unseen information and state the main idea in your own words without choices.
independent_check.passage: Beside each lift button, a small metal plate carries raised dots. A visitor feels the plates, matches the patterns she knows, and selects the correct floor independently.
independent_check.prompt: What is the main idea of this paragraph?

concept_slots.description: States that raised-dot labels identify lift floors or buttons by touch.
Explains that the labels help a blind reader choose a floor independently.
any_of: use the lift on her own

transfer_check.teaching_block: Transfer the same main-idea method to accessible packaging. Combine the label feature with its practical result.
transfer_check.passage: Two medicine boxes feel similar. One company adds distinct raised-dot names to each box. A customer reads the names with her fingers before choosing the prescribed medicine.
transfer_check.prompt: State the paragraph's main idea in your own words.

concept_slots.description: Mentions raised-dot or Braille names on medicine boxes.
Explains that the customer can identify or choose the correct medicine.

levels.title: Explain why an invention solves a need
levels.focus: infer a design purpose and support it with evidence
levels.teaching_goal: Connect a difficulty, a design choice, and its useful result in an evidence-backed reason.

guided_check.teaching_block: An invention reason has three links: problem, design, result. Worked example: printed signs cannot be read by touch, so raised symbols are added, allowing more people to read the information.
guided_check.passage: The library's shelf numbers were printed only in ink. Staff added raised-dot number labels so readers who use touch could find sections without waiting for help.
options: to let touch readers find sections independently
accepted_answers: to let touch readers find sections independently
so touch readers could find sections

bridge.teaching_block: Separate need from solution. Need: identify classroom rooms. Solution: place touch-readable signs at a reachable height.
bridge.passage: Rafi could not use signs placed high above the doors. The school fixed Braille room labels beside each handle.
bridge.prompt: Which detail shows how the school addressed Rafi's need?
options: labels were placed beside each handle
accepted_answers: labels were placed beside each handle

masterclass.teaching_block: Misconception check: saying 'because Braille is useful' is too vague. Name the exact barrier and explain how the feature removes it.
masterclass.passage: A bus timetable was available only behind glass. The depot added a durable touch-readable copy at hand level.
masterclass.prompt: Which answer gives the strongest reason for the change?
options: travellers who read by touch can check times themselves
glass is always the wrong material
accepted_answers: travellers who read by touch can check times themselves
touch readers can check times independently

independent_check.teaching_block: Explain the design choice in the unseen situation. Include both the access problem and the result.
independent_check.passage: The buttons on a new water dispenser felt identical. Designers added distinct raised symbols beside cold, normal, and warm so users could select safely by touch.
independent_check.prompt: Why do the raised symbols improve the dispenser?

concept_slots.description: Identifies that the buttons felt identical or could not be told apart by touch.
any_of: could not tell the buttons apart

concept_slots.description: Explains that users can identify temperatures and choose safely.

transfer_check.teaching_block: Apply problem-design-result reasoning to a tactile map rather than written labels.
transfer_check.passage: A park map used only coloured lines. A second map added raised paths, textured lawns, and a bumpy mark for each gate.
transfer_check.prompt: Explain why the second map gives better access, using evidence.
transfer_check.preflight_rule: The response must explain in English how tactile map features answer a touch reader's navigation need and cite at least one given feature.

rubric_criteria.description: Identifies that colour-only information is not accessible to every map reader.
Uses raised paths, textured lawns, or bumpy gate marks as evidence.
Explains how touch features help locate or follow places independently.

levels.title: Read access words in context
levels.focus: infer the meaning of tactile and invention vocabulary
levels.teaching_goal: Use nearby definitions and examples to understand raised, pattern, fingertip, tactile, and accessible.

guided_check.teaching_block: A definition clue may follow the word. Worked example: a raised mark stands above a flat surface, so a finger can feel it.
guided_check.passage: The raised dots stood slightly above the card instead of lying flat.

bridge.teaching_block: A pattern is an organised arrangement. Find the clue that tells how parts are placed, not what colour they are.
bridge.passage: The dots formed a pattern: two at the top, one in the middle, and none at the bottom.

masterclass.teaching_block: Misconception check: accessible does not merely mean nearby. Something accessible can be used or understood by people with different needs.
masterclass.passage: The museum made its guide accessible by offering large print, audio, and Braille versions.
masterclass.prompt: What does accessible mean in this sentence?
options: usable by people with different needs
accepted_answers: usable by people with different needs
easy for different people to use

independent_check.teaching_block: Use the unseen context to explain the word without choices.
independent_check.passage: The tactile diagram had rough rivers, smooth roads, and raised mountain lines that students could explore with their hands.

transfer_check.teaching_block: Transfer the word to a science activity and use the action clue.
transfer_check.passage: During the tactile sorting game, children closed their eyes and grouped shells by feeling their surfaces.
transfer_check.prompt: What does tactile tell you about the game?
accepted_answers: the game is done by feeling
objects are sorted by feeling them

levels.title: Use was and were with ongoing actions
levels.focus: match past-progressive grammar to singular and plural subjects
levels.teaching_goal: Use was or were plus an -ing verb to describe an action continuing at a past moment.

guided_check.teaching_block: Use was with one person or thing and were with more than one. Worked example: 'Asha was reading' has one reader; 'The students were reading' has several.
guided_check.passage: At ten o'clock, Kavya ___ tracing a Braille line with her fingertip.

bridge.teaching_block: Find the subject first. 'The volunteers' is plural, so choose were. Then keep the action in its -ing form.
bridge.passage: The volunteers ___ adding touch labels to the room doors.

masterclass.teaching_block: Misconception check: the nearest noun does not control the verb. The full subject does. In 'A box of labels was waiting', box is singular even though labels is plural.
masterclass.passage: A packet of Braille cards ___ lying beside the embosser.
masterclass.prompt: Which phrase agrees with the subject packet?

independent_check.teaching_block: Complete the unseen past-action sentence without choices.
independent_check.passage: When the bell rang, the two learners ___ reading the tactile notice.
independent_check.prompt: Write the correct two-word verb phrase.

transfer_check.teaching_block: Use the same tense pattern in a sports context. Write a complete sentence, not only the verb phrase.
transfer_check.passage: Past moment: sunset. Subject: one runner. Continuing action: practising on the track.
transfer_check.prompt: Write a complete sentence using was and the action.

concept_slots.description: Uses one runner as the subject.
Uses the past-progressive phrase was practising or was practicing.
Includes the track or sunset context.

levels.title: Compare reading formats in your own words
levels.focus: compare access features and summarise their shared purpose
levels.teaching_goal: Select relevant similarities and differences between Braille, print, and audio without ranking one reader's method above another.

guided_check.teaching_block: A comparison names what is similar and what is different. Worked example: print and Braille both record words; print is read mainly with sight, while Braille is read through raised patterns by touch.
guided_check.passage: A poem appears in dark ink on one page and in raised-dot cells on another. Both pages contain the same lines.
guided_check.prompt: Which comparison is accurate and respectful?
options: both carry the poem, but readers use different senses
only the ink page carries words
raised dots are pictures, not writing
every reader must use both pages
accepted_answers: both carry the poem, but readers use different senses
both have the poem but are read differently

bridge.teaching_block: Use a two-column plan: same purpose, different feature. Same purpose: share directions. Difference: audio is heard; Braille is felt.
bridge.passage: A station offers spoken platform announcements and Braille signs beside the stairs.
bridge.prompt: What shared purpose do both formats serve?

masterclass.teaching_block: Misconception check: compare features, not people's worth. Avoid saying one format is always better. The useful format depends on the reader and situation.
masterclass.passage: Dev listens to an audio story while cooking. Later, he reads its Braille recipe list quietly with both hands free from sound controls.
masterclass.prompt: Which conclusion best fits the evidence?
options: different formats can be useful in different situations
audio is always better than Braille
Braille can only be used in kitchens
a reader should choose only one format forever
accepted_answers: different formats can be useful in different situations
each format suits a different situation

independent_check.teaching_block: Compare the unseen formats in your own words. Include one shared purpose and one clear difference.
independent_check.passage: A seed packet gives planting steps in large print and Braille. Both versions list the same depth and watering time; one uses enlarged letters and the other raised dots.
independent_check.preflight_rule: The response must compare the two seed-packet formats in English using evidence from the passage and respectful wording.

rubric_criteria.description: States that both versions give the same planting information.
Contrasts enlarged print with raised-dot Braille.
Uses clear comparison language such as both, while, or but.
Expresses the comparison in original wording.

transfer_check.teaching_block: Transfer comparison to two non-reading tools. Summarise their common goal and different signals.
transfer_check.passage: At a crossing, a flashing symbol tells some pedestrians when to walk. A beeping signal gives the same timing through sound.
transfer_check.prompt: Compare the two signals in your own words.

concept_slots.description: States that both signals tell pedestrians when it is safe or time to cross.
Contrasts a visible flash with an audible beep.

items.passage: A board-game rule card has raised-dot instructions along its lower edge. Players who read through touch follow the same turns and scoring rules as other players.
items.prompt: Which main idea covers the paragraph?
options: touch-readable rules let more players use the same game
all board games have lower edges
accepted_answers: touch-readable rules let more players use the same game
braille rules make the game accessible

items.passage: At a clinic, numbered doors also carry raised-dot room names. Patients can feel the labels, locate the testing room, and move through the corridor with less assistance.
items.prompt: State the main idea in your own words.

concept_slots.description: Mentions raised-dot or touch-readable room labels.
Explains that patients can find rooms with greater independence.

items.passage: Rupa feels the title first, opens to the marked page, and reads the first Braille line with both index fingers.
items.prompt: What does Rupa do immediately after feeling the title?
options: she opens to the marked page
accepted_answers: she opens to the marked page

items.passage: The teacher places a tactile alphabet card on each desk. The class first explores one cell and then compares it with the next.
items.prompt: What does the class compare?
accepted_answers: one dot cell and the next

items.passage: The emergency exit sign was high and printed only. The hall added a Braille sign near the handrail.
items.prompt: Why is the new sign more useful to a touch reader?
options: it can be reached and read by touch
it changes where the exit is
accepted_answers: it can be reached and read by touch
it is reachable and touch readable

items.passage: A calendar has raised dots on important dates and a key explaining each pattern. Sameer checks the dates without asking someone to read them aloud.
items.prompt: Explain how the design supports Sameer's independence.

concept_slots.description: Mentions raised dots, patterns, or the tactile key.
Explains that Sameer can identify important dates without another reader.

items.passage: A hotel added Braille numbers beside room doors after guests reported that the identical handles gave no clue.
items.prompt: Complete the reason: The labels were needed because ___.
options: the handles did not identify the rooms by touch
accepted_answers: the handles did not identify the rooms by touch

items.passage: A science model labels the moon, Earth, and sun with distinct raised patterns beside each shape.
items.prompt: Write an evidence-backed reason for adding the patterns.

concept_slots.description: Names distinct raised patterns or tactile labels.
Explains that learners can identify or distinguish the three objects by touch.
any_of: know the moon earth and sun

items.passage: The embossed arrow rose above the flat plastic and could be felt clearly.
items.prompt: Which chapter word could replace embossed here?

items.passage: The dot arrangement for the letter was repeated on every practice card.
items.prompt: Write the word that means an organised arrangement.

items.passage: The accessible menu was offered in print, audio, and Braille so diners could choose a useful format.
items.prompt: What does accessible mean here?
options: usable by people with different needs
accepted_answers: usable by people with different needs
easy for different people to use

items.passage: The tactile puzzle uses rough, smooth, and bumpy pieces that players identify with their hands.
items.prompt: What does tactile mean in this context?

items.passage: At noon, the students ___ testing the new tactile globe.
items.prompt: Choose the correct past-progressive phrase.

items.passage: When the visitor arrived, one guide ___ explaining the Braille map.
items.prompt: Which past-progressive phrase completes the sentence about one guide?

items.passage: Subject: two children. Past action in progress: sorting tactile cards at the table.
items.prompt: Which is a complete sentence?
options: Two children were sorting tactile cards at the table.
Two children was sorting tactile cards.
accepted_answers: Two children were sorting tactile cards at the table.

items.passage: Past moment: evening. Subject: one librarian. Action: preparing Braille labels for new books.
items.prompt: Write one complete sentence using was and the action.

concept_slots.description: Names one librarian.
Uses was preparing.
Mentions Braille labels for new books.

items.passage: One weather report appears as large print on a screen. The same report is available as refreshable Braille on a touch device.
items.prompt: Which comparison is supported?
options: both give the same weather information in different forms
only the screen contains the report
the Braille device predicts different weather
both formats must be read by sight
accepted_answers: both give the same weather information in different forms

items.passage: A talking clock announces the time aloud. A tactile watch shows the time through raised markers under its cover.
items.prompt: Compare the shared purpose and one difference in your own words.

concept_slots.description: States that both tools tell or show the time.
Contrasts hearing the clock with feeling the watch.
any_of: one is heard and one is felt

items.passage: A bakery printed its price list, recorded an audio version, and added a Braille copy at the counter. Customers selected whichever version they could use most easily.
items.prompt: Which summary keeps the central idea?
options: The bakery offered the same prices in several accessible formats.
The bakery sold bread beside a counter.
Every customer listened to the same recording.
The printed list was the only useful one.
accepted_answers: The bakery offered the same prices in several accessible formats.

items.passage: A school election ballot has large print, clear audio instructions, and Braille candidate names. Each voter can review the same choices using a suitable format.
items.prompt: Summarise the design and its purpose in your own words.

concept_slots.description: Mentions multiple formats such as print, audio, and Braille.
Explains that voters can access the same choices in a suitable way.
